questions.explanation: Correct: inviting an external user creates a guest (B2B) user, not an internal member. The person gets an invitation email, accepts it, and joins the tenant as a guest. The first option describes creating an internal user. The other two confuse user types with service principals and managed identities.
options: An internal member user with a getwings.co address; no invitation is needed
A guest user (B2B); the person receives an invitation email and accepts it to join the tenant
A service principal; it can sign in but cannot be assigned roles
A managed identity; Azure manages its credentials automatically
questions.question: You invite a colleague's personal Outlook account to your tenant, getwings.co, to collaborate. What user type is created, and what happens next?
questions.source_quote: After you send the invitation, the user account is automatically added to the directory as a guest.
questions.source_title: Quickstart: Add a guest user and send an invitation

questions.explanation: Correct: Directory Reader is read-only for basic directory information. The guest can see properties in the Entra admin centre but cannot create users or edit properties. The other options all require a more privileged role such as User Administrator.
options: Read basic directory information, but not create users or edit user properties
Create new internal users and invite external users
Reset any user's password, including Global Administrators
Assign roles to other users
questions.question: You assign Directory Reader to the new guest user. What can that user do in the Entra admin centre?
questions.source_quote: There are about 60 Microsoft Entra built-in roles, which are roles with a fixed set of role permissions. To supplement the built-in roles, Microsoft Entra ID also supports custom roles.
questions.source_title: Understand Microsoft Entra role concepts - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: User Administrator is an Entra role for managing users in the directory — creating users, editing properties, resetting passwords. It does not grant Azure subscription access. Azure Owner is an Azure role, Storage Account Contributor is an Azure data-plane role, and Global Reader is a read-only Microsoft 365 role.
options: Azure Owner at subscription scope
User Administrator in Microsoft Entra ID
Storage Account Contributor at resource-group scope
Global Reader in Microsoft 365
questions.question: You need a user to create users and edit user properties, but not to manage Azure subscriptions. Which Entra role fits, and where is it assigned?
questions.source_quote: Azure has its own role-based access control system for Azure resources such as virtual machines, and this system is not the same as Microsoft Entra roles.
questions.source_title: Understand Microsoft Entra role concepts - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: this is the core Azure RBAC versus Entra RBAC distinction. An Entra role governs the directory and Microsoft 365. It does not give Azure Resource Manager permissions. Seeing no subscriptions in the Azure portal is the expected symptom of having no Azure role on that subscription — the fix is an Azure Reader assignment on the subscription. Signing in to the wrong tenant is possible in general, but the point here is the role-scope gap, and the user can see the tenant. User Administrator does not include Azure Owner. A Conditional Access policy does not grant authorisation.
options: The user is signed in to the wrong tenant
Entra roles do not grant Azure resource access — Azure RBAC is separate, and the user has no Azure role (for example, Reader) on the subscription
User Administrator automatically includes Azure Owner, so the portal must be broken
The user needs a Conditional Access policy before Azure resources appear
questions.question: A user has the Entra role User Administrator. They switch to the Azure portal in the same tenant and see no subscriptions or resources. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.source_quote: Azure has its own role-based access control system for Azure resources such as virtual machines, and this system is not the same as Microsoft Entra roles.
questions.source_title: Understand Microsoft Entra role concepts - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: Reader lets a user view all resources but not make changes. Creating and deleting storage accounts, assigning roles, and uploading blobs all require write or role-management permissions (Contributor, Owner, Role Based Access Control Administrator, or a data-plane role).
options: View all resources in the subscription, but not make changes
Create and delete storage accounts in the subscription
Assign roles to other users in the subscription
Upload blobs to any storage account in the subscription
questions.question: You assign Reader on a pay-as-you-go subscription to a guest user, as an active, permanent assignment. What can that user do?
questions.source_quote: A role assignment consists of three elements: security principal, role definition, and scope.
questions.source_title: What is Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)?

questions.explanation: Correct: PIM for Azure resources works the same way as PIM for Entra roles: make the role eligible, not standing. The user activates it from My Roles, provides a justification, the approver approves, and the role becomes Active for a limited window — after which the upload succeeds. A permanent active assignment keeps standing privilege, which PIM exists to remove. Global Administrator is excessive and still standing. A Conditional Access grant is not an RBAC permission.
options: Give them Storage Account Contributor permanently as an active assignment

Make Storage Account Contributor an eligible assignment on that storage account / resource group, with activation requiring justification and approval; the user activates it in My Roles, the approver approves, and the role moves to Active for a limited time
Give them Global Administrator permanently — it is the only role that can upload blobs
Create a Conditional Access policy requiring MFA; that alone grants upload permission
questions.question: A guest user has Reader on a subscription but cannot upload a blob to a storage account. You want them to be able to do it only when needed, with approval. What is the correct PIM approach?
questions.source_quote: Azure RBAC is an additive model, so your effective permissions are the sum of your role assignments.
questions.source_title: What is Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)?

questions.explanation: Correct: Entra custom roles can be scoped to the tenant, an administrative unit, or a single object. Azure custom roles can be scoped to management group, subscription, resource group, or resource. The first option denies Entra custom roles. The other two get the scopes backwards or too narrow.
options: Both are Azure custom roles — Entra does not support custom roles

Entra custom role scoped to the Finance administrative unit; Azure custom role scoped to that resource group. Entra custom roles can be scoped to tenant, administrative unit, or a single object; Azure custom roles to management group / subscription / resource group / resource
Both must be scoped tenant-wide — custom roles cannot be scoped narrower
Entra custom roles can only be scoped to a resource group; Azure custom roles only to a tenant
questions.question: You need a custom role that can reset passwords for users in the Finance administrative unit only, and a custom role that can manage VMs in one resource group only. Which is possible, and at what scope?
questions.source_quote: There are about 60 Microsoft Entra built-in roles, which are roles with a fixed set of role permissions. To supplement the built-in roles, Microsoft Entra ID also supports custom roles.
questions.source_title: Understand Microsoft Entra role concepts - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: least privilege is to replace Owner with the smallest role that does the job — Reader at subscription scope, or narrower — and to review and remediate the assignment. That is exactly the skill 'Evaluate and remediate overprivileged access assignments by using Azure RBAC.' Removing the user entirely is excessive. Making the Owner assignment eligible in PIM keeps standing Owner, which eligibility alone does not fix. Moving subscriptions ignores scope — Owner at a narrower scope is still Owner, but scope is the point of right-sizing.
options: Remove the user entirely — Owner cannot be reduced
Replace Owner with Reader at subscription scope (or a narrower scope), and review the assignment — this is 'Evaluate and remediate overprivileged access assignments by using Azure RBAC'
Make the Owner assignment eligible in PIM, but keep Owner at subscription scope permanently
Move the user to a different subscription — scope does not matter if the role is Owner
questions.question: Defender for Cloud flags a user with Owner at subscription scope who only reads cost reports. What is the least-privilege fix?
questions.source_quote: Azure RBAC is an additive model, so your effective permissions are the sum of your role assignments.
questions.source_title: What is Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)?

questions.explanation: Correct: a policy definition is a single rule; an initiative is a collection of policy definitions grouped for a goal such as a compliance standard; a policy assignment applies a definition or initiative at a scope — management group, subscription, resource group, or resource — and is inherited below that scope. An assignment is not the rule itself, an exemption is an exception, and blueprints and locks are different controls.
options: The single rule is a policy definition and the bundle is an initiative (a collection of policy definitions), both applied through a policy assignment at a scope such as a management group
The single rule is a policy assignment and the bundle is a policy definition
The single rule is a blueprint and the bundle is a resource lock
The single rule is an exemption and the bundle is a remediation task
questions.question: You need a rule that storage accounts must use private endpoints, applied to a whole management group, and a second rule that virtual machines must have disk encryption, applied with it as one bundle. Which Azure Policy concepts match the single rule and the bundle?
questions.source_quote: Azure Policy evaluates resources and actions in Azure by comparing the properties of those resources to business rules. These business rules, described in JSON format, are known as policy definitions. To simplify management, several business rules can be grouped together to form a policy initiative, also referred to as a policySet.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy - Azure Policy

questions.explanation: Correct: Audit allows the request but logs a compliance warning and marks the resource non-compliant, giving visibility without blocking — the standard safe rollout before switching to Deny. Deny blocks matching create/update requests but does not delete existing resources. DeployIfNotExists deploys a missing related resource, it does not delete a public IP. Disabled means the rule is not evaluated at all.
options: DeployIfNotExists, which deletes the public IP automatically on existing VMs
Audit, which allows the request to proceed but records the resource as non-compliant so you can measure impact before enforcing
Deny, which blocks the deployment and deletes existing non-compliant VMs
Disabled, which enforces the rule silently without logging
questions.question: You want to roll out a new rule — virtual machines must not have a public IP — but you are not yet sure how many existing deployments it would break. What is the safe first effect to use, and what does it do?
questions.source_quote: Start with an audit or auditIfNotExists effect instead of an enforcement (deny, modify, deployIfNotExists) effect to track how your policy definition affects the resources in your environment.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy - Azure Policy

questions.explanation: Correct: CanNotDelete lets authorised users read and modify a resource but not delete it — right for production. ReadOnly lets users read but not delete or update, similar to restricting everyone to Reader permissions — right for the archive. The swapped answer would block production updates and allow archive changes. The two locks are not equivalent, and CanNotDelete does block deletion.
options: ReadOnly on both; CanNotDelete still allows deletion by an Owner
ReadOnly on the production group and CanNotDelete on the archived group
CanNotDelete on the production group and ReadOnly on the archived group
CanNotDelete on both; ReadOnly and CanNotDelete do the same thing
questions.question: A production resource group holds a storage account that must never be deleted, but engineers must still be able to update its configuration. A second, archived resource group must not be changed or deleted at all. Which locks fit?
questions.source_quote: CanNotDelete means authorized users can read and modify a resource, but they can't delete it. ReadOnly means authorized users can read a resource, but they can't delete or update it. Applying this lock is similar to restricting all authorized users to the permissions that the Reader role provides.
questions.source_title: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure - Azure Resource Manager

questions.explanation: Correct: Deny affects future requests — it rejects matching creates/updates and marks existing matches non-compliant, but it does not change them. Compliance evaluation alone never corrects existing resources; only a remediation task, for a modify or deployIfNotExists policy, changes what is already deployed. Deny never deletes resources, and scope does not change this behaviour.
options: Yes — Deny remediates existing resources on the next compliance evaluation

No — Deny only blocks future create and update requests; existing non-compliant resources stay non-compliant until a remediation task runs, and only modify or deployIfNotExists policies support remediation tasks that change existing resources
No — Deny deletes the existing storage accounts at the next evaluation
Yes, but only if the policy is assigned at management group scope; at subscription scope Deny cannot remediate
questions.question: You assign a Deny policy that blocks storage accounts without private endpoints. A week later, 40 existing storage accounts still have public endpoints and are marked non-compliant. An engineer says the Deny policy will fix them automatically at the next evaluation cycle, about 24 hours later. Is that right, and what actually fixes them?
questions.source_quote: The standard compliance evaluation cycle that occurs once every 24 hours.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy - Azure Policy

questions.explanation: Correct: Modify adds, replaces, or removes tags and properties on create/update, and deployIfNotExists deploys a template when a related resource is missing — both are the effects that can remediate, and both require a managed identity on the assignment (the deployment or modification uses the assignment's identity). Audit and auditIfNotExists only report and need no identity. Append is the older, narrower option Microsoft recommends replacing with modify for tags, and Deny blocks rather than adding anything.
options: Modify for the tag and deployIfNotExists for diagnostics; both need a managed identity on the assignment so the change or deployment can be performed, while audit needs no identity
Append for the tag and auditIfNotExists for diagnostics; neither needs anything extra
Audit for both; a remediation task supplies the managed identity automatically
Deny for the tag and modify for diagnostics; only Deny needs a managed identity
questions.question: You need a policy that adds a missing 'CostCenter' tag to resources at creation, and a second policy that deploys diagnostic settings where they are missing. Which effects do you use, and what does each assignment need that an audit policy does not?
questions.source_quote: The managed identity of a deployIfNotExists or modify policy assignment needs enough permissions to create or update targeted resources.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy - Azure Policy

questions.explanation: Correct: an exemption is a documented, time-limited exception for specific resources, with an expiry after which compliance evaluation resumes — the governed way to allow one legacy VM temporarily. An exclusion removes a scope (such as a resource group) from the assignment itself. The terms are not interchangeable: exemption is per-resource and expiring, exclusion is a scope carve-out on the assignment. Deleting the assignment removes the control for everyone, and a remediation task fixes resources rather than excepting them.
options: A remediation task for the VM and a Deny policy for the resource group
Exclusion for the VM and exemption for the resource group — the two terms are interchangeable
Delete the policy assignment for both; exceptions cannot be scoped to a single resource
Exemption for the VM (time-bound, with an expiry date and a reason, scoped to that resource) and an exclusion on the assignment scope for the resource group
questions.question: A hospital has a legacy VM that cannot meet the 'allowed VM SKUs' policy. The team wants a documented, time-limited exception for that one VM, after which the policy applies again — without changing the assignment for everyone else. A second team wants a whole resource group permanently left out of the policy. Which mechanisms fit each need?
questions.source_quote: An assignment is a policy definition or initiative that was assigned to a specific scope. This scope could range from a management group to an individual resource. All child resources inherit the assignments. However, you can exclude a subscope from the assignment.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy - Azure Policy

questions.explanation: Correct: Entra roles and Azure roles are separate RBAC systems — different data stores for role definitions and assignments, and different policy decision points for access checks. The other options wrongly merge the two systems or invent a sync that does not exist.
options: They are the same system with two names — a role in one is automatically a role in the other
Entra roles are a subset of Azure roles, stored in the same data store
Azure roles are evaluated by the Entra policy decision point, and Entra roles by Azure Resource Manager
They are separate RBAC systems with different data stores for role definitions and assignments and different policy decision points for access checks
questions.question: A new administrator assumes that assigning an Entra role and assigning an Azure role are two views of the same permission system. What is the correct model?
questions.source_quote: When we say separate role-based access control system, it means there is a different data store where role definitions and role assignments are stored. Similarly, there is a different policy decision point where access checks happen.
questions.source_title: Understand Microsoft Entra role concepts - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: Entra built-in roles fall into three categories — Entra ID-specific roles (User Administrator, Application Administrator, Groups Administrator), service-specific roles (Exchange, Intune, SharePoint, Teams Administrators), and cross-service roles (Global Administrator, Global Reader, Security Administrator, Security Reader). The other options invent categories or deny the structure.
options: There is only one category — all Entra roles work the same way everywhere
Entra roles are divided into Reader and Writer only
Entra ID-specific roles, service-specific roles, and cross-service roles
Entra roles are divided by licence: P1 roles, P2 roles, and free roles
questions.question: An architect is mapping which Entra roles can manage which services. How are Entra built-in roles categorised?
questions.source_quote: Microsoft Entra built-in roles differ in where they can be used, which fall into the following three broad categories: Microsoft Entra ID-specific roles, Service-specific roles in Microsoft Entra ID, Cross-service roles in Microsoft Entra ID.
questions.source_title: Understand Microsoft Entra role concepts - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: Global Administrator and Global Reader are the two global cross-service roles — all Microsoft 365 services honour them. Security Administrator and Security Reader are cross-service security roles, not global ones. User Administrator is Entra ID-specific, and Exchange Administrator is service-specific.
options: User Administrator and Helpdesk Administrator
Exchange Administrator and SharePoint Administrator
Security Administrator and Security Reader
Global Administrator and Global Reader
questions.question: Which two Entra roles are the global cross-service roles that all Microsoft 365 services honour?
questions.source_quote: We have two global roles - Global Administrator and Global Reader. All Microsoft 365 services honor these two roles.
questions.source_title: Understand Microsoft Entra role concepts - Microsoft Entra ID

questions.explanation: Correct: a role assignment consists of three elements — security principal, role definition, and scope. Without all three there is no assignment. The other options omit an element or add one that is not part of the assignment.
options: User, password, and subscription
Role definition and scope only — the principal is implied
Security principal, role definition, and scope
Security principal, Conditional Access policy, and licence
questions.question: An auditor asks what an Azure role assignment is made of. Which three elements must it contain?
questions.source_quote: A role assignment consists of three elements: security principal, role definition, and scope.
questions.source_title: What is Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)?

questions.explanation: Correct: a security principal is a user, group, service principal, or managed identity requesting access — any of these can hold a role assignment. It is not limited to human users, and it is not the role definition or the scope.
options: Only a human user can be a security principal
Only a group can be a security principal
A security principal is the role definition itself
A user, group, service principal, or managed identity requesting access to Azure resources
questions.question: A runbook's managed identity needs Reader on a resource group. A colleague says only users and groups can be security principals. Is that right?
questions.source_quote: A security principal is an object that represents a user, group, service principal, or managed identity that is requesting access to Azure resources. You can assign a role to any of these security principals.
questions.source_title: What is Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)?

questions.explanation: Correct: scope can be set at four levels — management group, subscription, resource group, or resource — in a parent-child structure, and roles can be assigned at any level. There is no tenant-wide Azure RBAC scope and no fifth level.
options: Three levels: subscription, resource group, or resource
Two levels: subscription or resource group
Four levels: management group, subscription, resource group, or resource
Five levels: tenant, management group, subscription, resource group, or resource
questions.question: You need to give a team Contributor on one resource group only, not the whole subscription. At how many levels can Azure RBAC scope be set, and which are they?
questions.source_quote: In Azure, you can specify a scope at four levels: management group, subscription, resource group, or resource. Scopes are structured in a parent-child relationship. You can assign roles at any of these levels of scope.
questions.source_title: What is Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)?

questions.explanation: Correct: Azure RBAC is an additive model — effective permissions are the sum of the assignments, so the Reader assignment adds nothing on top of Contributor at the subscription scope. There is no 'most restrictive wins' rule for overlapping allow assignments, and the narrower assignment does not cancel the broader one.
options: The Reader assignment overrides Contributor, so the user can only read
The two assignments cancel each other out and the user has no access
The narrower scope wins, so the user can only read inside the resource group
Effective permissions are the sum of the assignments, so the user effectively has Contributor across the subscription and the Reader assignment has no impact
questions.question: A user has Contributor at subscription scope and Reader on one resource group in that subscription. What are their effective permissions?
questions.source_quote: Azure RBAC is an additive model, so your effective permissions are the sum of your role assignments.
questions.source_title: What is Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)?

questions.explanation: Correct: role assignments are transitive for groups — if a user is in a group, and that group is in another group that has the role assignment, the user has the permissions. The other options deny transitivity or invent a direct-membership-only rule.
options: The user has no permissions — only direct members of the assigned group count
The user has permissions only if they are also directly assigned the role
The user has the permissions, because role assignments are transitive for groups
The user has the permissions only during the first 24 hours after joining the nested group
questions.question: A user is a member of Group A. Group A is a member of Group B. Group B has Contributor on a resource group. Does the user have Contributor permissions?
questions.source_quote: Role assignments are transitive for groups, which means that if a user is a member of a group and that group is a member of another group that has a role assignment, the user has the permissions in the role assignment.
questions.source_title: What is Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)?

questions.explanation: Correct: effective permissions are computed as Actions minus NotActions (and DataActions minus NotDataActions) — a wildcard allow with a subtraction for the excluded actions. The other options ignore NotActions, treat wildcards as unlimited, or invent a deny-by-default for data actions.
options: The wildcard grants everything, including the excluded actions — NotActions is only advisory
NotActions only applies to data actions, not management actions
The role grants nothing, because a wildcard and a NotActions entry cancel each other out
Effective permissions are Actions minus NotActions — the wildcard allows everything except the actions listed in NotActions
questions.question: A custom role allows Microsoft.Storage/* but lists Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/delete in NotActions. What can a holder of this role do?
questions.source_quote: Actions - NotActions = Effective management permissions. DataActions - NotDataActions = Effective data permissions.
questions.source_title: What is Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)?

questions.explanation: Correct: Azure RBAC checks deny assignments first — if a deny assignment applies, access is blocked, and evaluation does not continue to the allow assignments. A deny assignment is not outranked by Owner, not limited to one scope, and not advisory.
options: The Owner assignment wins, because Owner outranks deny assignments
The deny assignment is only advisory and is logged, not enforced
If a deny assignment applies, access is blocked — deny is evaluated before the allow assignments
The two assignments are summed, so the user keeps half their permissions
questions.question: A user has Owner on a subscription, but a deny assignment applies to a storage account in that subscription. Can the user delete the storage account?
questions.source_quote: If a deny assignment applies, access is blocked. Otherwise, evaluation continues.
questions.source_title: What is Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)?

questions.explanation: Correct: Azure RBAC is free and included in the Azure subscription — there is no per-user RBAC licence. The other options invent a P1/P2 requirement or a per-assignment charge.
options: Azure RBAC requires Entra ID P1 for every user with a role assignment
Azure RBAC requires Entra ID P2 for every user with a role assignment
Azure RBAC is charged per role assignment per month
Azure RBAC is free and included in the Azure subscription
questions.question: Finance asks whether the Azure RBAC rollout needs a new licence budget. What is the licensing position?
questions.source_quote: Using this feature is free and included in your Azure subscription.
questions.source_title: What is Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)?

questions.explanation: Correct: Azure Policy evaluates resource state against business rules without concern for who made the change or who has permission to make it — that is the Policy versus RBAC distinction. RBAC manages user actions at scopes; Policy ensures the resulting resource state is compliant. The other options assign Policy the RBAC job or vice versa.
options: Azure Policy controls who can perform an action, and Azure RBAC checks the resulting resource state
Azure Policy and Azure RBAC do the same thing, so only one is needed
Azure Policy evaluates resource state against business rules without concern for who made the change; Azure RBAC focuses on managing user actions at different scopes
Azure Policy only works if the user has no RBAC role at all
questions.question: An engineer with Contributor creates a storage account without a private endpoint, and the creation is blocked. They have the RBAC permission to create storage accounts. Which control blocked it, and why?
questions.source_quote: Azure Policy ensures that resource state is compliant to your business rules without concern for who made the change or who has permission to make a change. Azure RBAC focuses on managing user actions at different scopes. If control of an action is required based on user information, then Azure RBAC is the correct tool to use. Even if an individual has access to perform an action, if the result is a non-compliant resource, Azure Policy still blocks the create or update.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy - Azure Policy

questions.explanation: Correct: all Policy objects — definitions, initiatives, and assignments — are readable to all roles over their scope, by design, so everyone can see what rules are set. The other options invent a read restriction, a P2 requirement, or a hidden-by-default model.
options: Policy objects are visible only to Owners
Policy objects are visible only to users with a P2 licence
Policy definitions are hidden from Readers by default
All Policy objects, including definitions, initiatives, and assignments, are readable to all roles over their scope
questions.question: A Reader on a subscription wants to see which Azure Policy assignments apply to their resource group. Can they?
questions.source_quote: All Policy objects, including definitions, initiatives, and assignments, are readable to all roles over its scope. For example, a Policy assignment scoped to an Azure subscription is readable by all role holders at the subscription scope and lower.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy - Azure Policy

questions.explanation: Correct: Policy evaluates at resource creation or update, when a scope gets a new assignment, when an assigned policy or initiative is updated, and in the standard compliance evaluation cycle every 24 hours. It does not evaluate only at creation, only on demand, or only weekly.
options: Only when a resource is created — never again
Only when an administrator manually triggers an evaluation
At resource creation or update, when a scope gets a new assignment, when an assigned policy is updated, and in the standard 24-hour compliance evaluation cycle
Only once a week, on Sundays
questions.question: A non-compliant storage account was created before a policy was assigned. When will Policy evaluate it?
questions.source_quote: Resources are evaluated at specific times during the resource lifecycle, the policy assignment lifecycle, and for regular ongoing compliance evaluation. A resource is created or updated in a scope with a policy assignment. A scope gets a new assignment of a policy or initiative. A policy or initiative already assigned to a scope is updated. The standard compliance evaluation cycle that occurs once every 24 hours.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy - Azure Policy

questions.explanation: Correct: the managed identity of a deployIfNotExists or modify assignment needs enough permissions to create or update the targeted resources — without them the remediation cannot run. An audit assignment needs no identity, and the identity does not need Owner on everything, nor is the identity optional for these effects.
options: No identity is needed — remediation runs with the user's permissions
The assignment needs the Global Administrator role
The assignment needs a managed identity with Reader on the subscription only
The assignment's managed identity needs enough permissions to create or update the targeted resources
questions.question: A deployIfNotExists policy is assigned but its remediation tasks keep failing with authorisation errors. What is the most likely cause?
questions.source_quote: The managed identity of a deployIfNotExists or modify policy assignment needs enough permissions to create or update targeted resources.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy - Azure Policy

questions.explanation: Correct: the Resource Policy Contributor role includes most Azure Policy operations, and Owner has full rights; Contributor has read access but cannot create or update definitions and assignments, and Reader has read access only. User Access Administrator is needed to grant the managed identity on deployIfNotExists or modify assignments.
options: The Resource Policy Contributor role includes most Azure Policy operations, and Owner has full rights
Any Contributor can create and update policy definitions and assignments
Only Global Administrators can read policy assignments
The Reader role can create policy assignments but not definitions
questions.question: Who can create and manage Azure Policy definitions and assignments?
questions.source_quote: Many built-in roles grant permission to Azure Policy resources. The Resource Policy Contributor role includes most Azure Policy operations. Owner has full rights. Both Contributor and Reader have access to all read Azure Policy operations.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy - Azure Policy

questions.explanation: Correct: definitions at higher levels such as management group or subscription, with the assignment at the next child level, is the recommended pattern — and initiatives should be used even for a single definition so more can be added later without new assignments. Creating everything at the resource level, or one assignment per resource, is the anti-pattern.
options: Create definitions at the resource level and assign them one resource at a time
Create one assignment per resource and never use initiatives
Create definitions at higher levels such as management group or subscription, assign at the next child level, and use initiative definitions even when starting with a single policy definition
Create definitions only at the tenant level and never assign below it
questions.question: Your team is designing an Azure Policy hierarchy for 50 subscriptions. What structure does Microsoft recommend?
questions.source_quote: We recommend creating definitions at higher levels such as the management group or subscription level. Then, create the assignment at the next child level. We recommend creating and assigning initiative definitions even if starting with a single policy definition.
questions.source_title: Overview of Azure Policy - Azure Policy

questions.explanation: Correct: a lock overrides any user permissions — even an Owner cannot delete or modify past a lock they do not remove first. The lock applies across all users and roles, unlike RBAC which grants permissions per user. The other options wrongly assume Owner or Global Administrator bypasses locks.
options: The Owner can delete the storage account — locks do not apply to Owners
The Global Administrator can override any lock without removing it
The Contributor can delete it if they also hold Reader
No one can delete it while the lock is in place — the lock overrides any user permissions, including Owner
questions.question: A storage account has a CanNotDelete lock. An Owner tries to delete it. What happens?
questions.source_quote: As an administrator, you can lock an Azure subscription, resource group, or resource to protect them from accidental user deletions and modifications. The lock overrides any user permissions.
questions.source_title: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure - Azure Resource Manager

questions.explanation: Correct: locks only apply to control plane operations, not data plane operations — a ReadOnly lock on a storage account does not protect blob, queue, table, or file data from deletion through the data plane. The control plane protects the resource itself; the data plane is a separate path. The other options confuse the two planes.
options: The blobs are protected — a ReadOnly lock blocks all deletions everywhere
The blobs are protected only if the user is not an Owner
Locks only apply to control plane operations, not data plane operations, so blob data can still be deleted through the data plane
The lock protects data only for 24 hours, then expires
questions.question: A storage account has a ReadOnly lock. A user with Storage Blob Data Contributor deletes blobs through the storage data plane. Are the blobs protected by the lock?
questions.source_quote: Locks only apply to control plane Azure operations and not to data plane operations. A read-only lock or cannot-delete lock on a storage account doesn't protect its data from being deleted or modified.
questions.source_title: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure - Azure Resource Manager

questions.explanation: Correct: when a lock is applied at a parent scope, all resources within that scope inherit it — even resources added later — and the most restrictive lock in the inheritance chain takes precedence. A child lock does not cancel a parent lock, and new resources are not exempt.
options: All resources in the group inherit the lock, including resources added later, and the most restrictive lock in the chain takes precedence
Only resources that existed when the lock was created are locked; new resources are exempt
A lock on a child resource cancels the parent lock for that resource
Locks do not inherit — each resource must be locked individually
questions.question: You apply a ReadOnly lock at the resource-group scope. A week later an engineer creates a new VM in that group. Is the VM locked?
questions.source_quote: When you apply a lock at a parent scope, all resources within that scope inherit the same lock. Even resources you add later inherit the same parent lock. The most restrictive lock in the inheritance chain takes precedence.
questions.source_title: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure - Azure Resource Manager

questions.explanation: Correct: if a Delete lock is on a resource and you attempt to delete its resource group, the feature blocks the whole delete operation — even if the group and other resources are unlocked, a partial deletion is not possible. The lock does not only protect the single resource, and it is not bypassed by deleting the group.
options: The resource group is deleted except for the locked resource
The locked resource is deleted but the group remains
The deletion succeeds because the lock is on the resource, not the group
The whole delete operation is blocked — a partial deletion is not possible
questions.question: A resource group contains a storage account with a Delete (CanNotDelete) lock. An Owner tries to delete the entire resource group. What happens?
questions.source_quote: If you have a Delete lock on a resource and attempt to delete its resource group, the feature blocks the whole delete operation. Even if the resource group or other resources in the resource group are unlocked, the deletion doesn't happen. A partial deletion isn't possible.
questions.source_title: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure - Azure Resource Manager

questions.explanation: Correct: creating or deleting management locks needs Microsoft.Authorization/* or Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* — Owner and User Access Administrator have it. Contributor does not, Reader does not, and a custom role needs those actions explicitly.
options: Any Contributor can create or delete locks
Any Reader can create locks but not delete them
Owner and User Access Administrator have the required access (Microsoft.Authorization/locks/*); a Contributor does not
Only Global Administrators can create or delete locks
questions.question: A Contributor tries to add a CanNotDelete lock to a production resource group and gets an authorisation error. Who can create or delete management locks?
questions.source_quote: To create or delete management locks, you need access to Microsoft.Authorization/* or Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* actions. Users assigned to the Owner and the User Access Administrator roles have the required access.
questions.source_title: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure - Azure Resource Manager

questions.explanation: Correct: a ReadOnly lock on a resource group prevents starting or restarting a VM, because those operations require a POST to the Resource Manager API, which the lock blocks. The other options invent exceptions for Owners, for running VMs, or for stop operations.
options: Starting the VM works — ReadOnly locks only block deletions
Starting the VM works for Owners, who bypass ReadOnly locks
Starting the VM works if the VM is already running, but not if it is stopped
Starting or restarting the VM is blocked, because those operations require a POST request that a ReadOnly lock blocks
questions.question: A resource group has a ReadOnly lock. An engineer tries to start a stopped VM in that group. What happens?
questions.source_quote: A read-only lock on a resource group that contains a virtual machine prevents all users from starting or restarting a virtual machine. These operations require a POST method request.
questions.source_title: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure - Azure Resource Manager

questions.explanation: Correct: a ReadOnly lock on a storage account prevents listing the account keys, because List Keys is a POST to the Resource Manager API, and the keys give complete access to the data. Users without the keys must use Entra credentials to access blob or queue data. The lock does not hand out the keys, does not only block Owners, and does not expire.
options: Listing the account keys is blocked, because it is a POST request the ReadOnly lock stops — users without the keys must use Microsoft Entra credentials to access the data
Listing the keys works — ReadOnly locks only block data plane operations
Listing the keys works for Owners, who bypass the lock
The keys are automatically rotated when a ReadOnly lock is applied
questions.question: A storage account has a ReadOnly lock. A user with Reader tries to list the account keys in the portal. What happens?
questions.source_quote: A read-only lock on a storage account prevents users from listing the account keys. A POST request handles the Azure Storage List Keys operation to protect access to the account keys. The account keys provide complete access to data in the storage account. When a read-only lock is configured for a storage account, users who don't have the account keys need to use Microsoft Entra credentials to access blob or queue data.
questions.source_title: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure - Azure Resource Manager

questions.explanation: Correct: locks cannot be added to management groups — the portal and API do not support it. They can be applied to subscriptions, resource groups, and resources. The other options invent a management-group lock capability.
options: A management group can be locked with a ReadOnly lock
A management group can be locked with a CanNotDelete lock
You can't add a lock to management groups — locks apply to subscriptions, resource groups, and resources
A management group lock requires a P2 licence, but is otherwise supported
questions.question: Your governance team wants a ReadOnly lock on the top-level management group to freeze the whole hierarchy. Is that possible?
questions.source_quote: You can't add a lock to management groups.
questions.source_title: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure - Azure Resource Manager

questions.explanation: Correct: unlike RBAC, management locks apply a restriction across all users and roles — that is the point of a lock versus a permission. RBAC grants per-user permissions; a lock restricts everyone, including Owners, until it is removed. The other options describe RBAC, not locks.
options: Locks grant permissions to specific users, like RBAC roles do
Locks only apply to guest users, not members
Locks are the same as deny assignments in Azure RBAC
Unlike RBAC, management locks apply a restriction across all users and roles
questions.question: A junior admin asks how a resource lock differs from simply removing everyone's RBAC roles on the resource. What is the key difference?
questions.source_quote: Unlike with role-based access control (RBAC), you use management locks to apply a restriction across all users and roles.
